Yes ſir, and this is the old Gentleman himſelfe, and ſomebody has ſtole away his habite to abuſe him. If any man be ſo hardy, let him take his chance. Then you will make his mouth as unſerviceable as your fathers gumm'd velvet. I imagin'd there would be a great deale of blood ſpilt in the skirmiſh, and ſo I brought theſe to wipe the wounds, nothing elſe ſir: looke you here they come. Preſſe that point home. Seize her for fellons goods, ſhe belongs to the Lord of the ſoyle. He lyes, beat him for lying, what doe you ſtay for? Let's bind him faſt, and then lay him upon his backe, and geld him. You muſt not be too ſudden now in the opening of your plot, after you have marryed them. Why before you reveale your proceedings, you ſhall preſent your ſelfe with a great deale of confidence, and pro miſe of deſert; walke up and downe, with a joyfull agony, and a trembling joy, as if you had eſcapt from a breach, or re deem'd your country: then when you ſee them ſufficiently fill'd with expectation, you may draw the curtaine of your valour, and ſtound them with admiration. To a foole. Tis all one.
speeches.Lit: Crochet you know, that I am determind to marry my other daughter Aemilia, to old Dotario the Citizen. So much the worſe, when tis corrupted: marke mee what I ſay, giue him the reines, and if Fidlers ſleepe in a weeke, Tavernes keepe their doores ſhut, the Conſtable ſit on a ſtall in peace, or wenches walke the ſtreets for him (if he be like his father) nere credit me againe. Why whats the matter
Good ſir, thinke your power may command my du ty, but not my affection. You know ſir, the incovenience ſtill happens to theſe forc'd matches, they never come to good, and if you compell mee to like of him, you muſt expect the ſame iſſue, you ſhall neuer make mee any other preſident. I ſhall never love him. Oh mee, what ſhall I doe? would my life were a ſacrifice. Prethee what good? Thy mirth comes importunely on my greife. I perceive it well enough Crochet. I thinke the foole will be tedious. Truly I have no skill to make any conjecture by the outward appeareance, but by the Title page of your face, I ſhould judge you to be ſomewhat ancient. O tis worme eaten, time has cankerd it, beſides there be ſo many daſhes, my vnderſtanding will not ſerve mee to reade it, and a woman has no vſe of her Clergy. How long is it ſince the coppy has beene al ter'd? Sweete Lady, what a petulant word is there, for a man of your beard? a Boy of fifteene would not have ſpoke it without bluſhing, and ther's a ſmile able to turne my ſtomack. I wonder you will make your ſelfe ſo ridiculous. Now you are alone, Ile tell you what I thinke of you, you are an old doting foole, one that twenty yeares ſince, has drunke the Lethe of humanity, and forgot of what ſexe thou wert, worne out of all remembrance of thy ſelfe, thou haſt a body, that a feaver cannot heat, nor poy ſon worke upon, a face more rugged then winter, thy beard is moſſe, and thy skin ſo hard, that the perpetuall dropping of thy noſe cannot ſoften it. And yet you would bee in loue forſooth, whom Cu pid with all his ſtrength is not able to pierce, you haue not one pore open to let in an Arrow, more need haue a cordiall to comfort you. If you had any. Yes and if I marry you, Ile uſe you accordingly, Ile haue no mercy on thy age, I tell you before hand, that when it happens, it may not ſeeme ſtrange to you. Doe but heare what I ſay to you, and it ſhall fall out, no Prognoſtication like it. When I am your wife, if you are ſo hardy to ven ter on me, your whole ſtudy ſhall be to pleaſe me, and yet I will not grace it with acceptance; I will liue as your Em preſſe, lye a bed, and command you, and your ſervants, and you ſhall not dare to anger me. No if you doe, I will fill the houſe with noyſe, and deafe thee with clamours. Hee will not be put off, I muſt terrifie him farther: and for your eſtate, you ſhall not meddle with it, Ile take up your rents for you, and diſpoſe of them, as I thinke fit; onely Ile allow you to carry ſome farthings in your pouch to giue to Beggers. For the reſt, Ile ſpend it upon my ſelfe in bravery: there ſhall not be a new faſhion, but Ile haue it. Ile looke af ter nothing elſe; your houſe ſhall be a mart for all trades. Ile keepe twenty continually at worke for me; as Taylors, Perfu mers, Painters, Apothecaries, Coach-makers, Sempſters, and Tire-women. Beſides Embroyderers, and Penſions for in telligencers. Beſides, I will haue acquaintance with all the La dies in Court, and entertaine them with banquets, yet for all that I will make my complaint of you to them, traduce your infirmities, and they ſhall conſpire againſt you, and pitty mee. Then you ſhall kiſſe mee very ſeldome, and when I vouchſafe you the favour: and you ſhall doe it not as a huſ band, but as a father, not a ſmacke of laſciviouſneſſe. I will lye with you the firſt yeare once a moneth, as a Parſon vſes to inſtruct his Cure, and yet not bee queſtion'd for neglect, or non reſidence: marry the next yeare, if you liue ſo long, once a quarter ſhall ſuffice you. Theſe are the leaſt of your evils. I will haue one to cuckold you, and you ſhall take it for a curteſie, and uſe him the kindlier for it. Maſter Careleſſe promis'd to bee here inſtantly. Ile tell him what a fine youth he has to his Vncle. Saue you Maſter Careleſſe. Whence come you, from Apollo? I thought I had beene worthy ſalutation. Where I loue, I will not ſtand upon conditions. Doe you want money? I haue not ready coyne; but there's a jewell Will fetch you twenty pound. I giue it freely. Why doe you aske? Becauſe they ſay that ſtone Has ſecret vertue in it to recover, A man that's intoxicated, and I doe find That I am not ſo drunke, as I was. If hee could get it. I made ſuch ſport with him, and terrified him, how I would uſe him if I were his wife, That he is frighted hence. COme ſiſter, though our liberty be ſtraightned, Our mind ſtands free, without compulſion, There's none can make a rape upon our will. Well if they underſtood a women truely, They would not ſeeke to curbe ſo, whoſe nature Rejoyces like a torrent, to make way Spight of impediments. Now if their wiſedome Should let us alone, we might perhaps our ſelues Find out the inconvenience, and prevent it, Which they like a falſe perſpectiue would ſeeke, To multiply upon us. I would not haue you leaue him, Nor yet turne deſperate. Now would I rather Get him by ſome deviſe, I loue a witty And an ingenuous tricke aboue my life: And ſhould take more delight to over-reach them, Then to enjoy my purpoſe. Come feare it not. You ſee what a man they would put upon me, Might be my father. H' has leſſe vigour in him, Then any Catamite. There's not reſeru'd So much as one maſculine graine in him. A fellow that's as bald, as a Lookinglaſſe, And whoſe diſeaſes are beyond Arithmeticke: Not a joynt of him free, a gowty numneſſe Has ſeiz'd his feete and fingers, and there's all The ſtiffeneſſe he has left: and were I married I muſt ſpend all my life in rubbing of him With hot wollen cloaths, and applying Plaiſters, And Cataplaſmes, and trenchers to his belly; Muſt undergoe the perſon of a Chirurgion, Not of a wife: and yet I am not terrified: It moues me not, I make a jeaſt of it; Becauſe I meane t' abuſe them all, and chuſe Where I like beſt. Like me; thou haſt not ſtudied thy ſelfe ſo well: Nor haſt that ſeaſon of thy mother in thee. Obſerue her faſhions, take example by them: Although her husband be penurious, Hard as the mettle, that he dotes upon. Yet ſhe can make him mallemable, and worke him, And turne, and hammer him, and wire-draw him, And rule him with as much correction, As one would wiſh to governe. For my part; When I haue ſtretcht my braines, made all the ſhifts, The wit of woman can be pregnant of. And ſhew'd my loue by ſuch experience, As ſhall outſtrip beliefe, all for his ſake That ſhall enioy me, which is Maſter Careleſſe. And when he has me, if hee ſhall preſume, On former paſſages of my affection, To overſway me in the leaſt deſire, To contradict, and tempt my patience, Ile ſhake off all obedience, and forget it. Ile ſlight him, yet prevaile. You are a foole, And every one that will can make you ſo: When was your ſweet heart Maſter Spruſe here with you? Take heed, What ere he ſpeakes, it tends but to corrupt you, I'de ioyne commerce of language with a Sphinx, Ere I'de daigne to anſwer him. Maſter Careleſſe Told me his humours, ſeemes he boaſted of it, He gaue his character, the moſt perfideous, And loue abuſing creature in the world; That all his vowes were treacherous: his ſmiles, His words, and actions, like ſmall Rivulets, Through twenty turnings of looſe paſſions, At laſt would runne to the dead ſea of ſinne. Bee wiſe, and conſtant, and then governe fate: And in the interim, how ere matters fall, Wee I find a tricke wench, how to cheat them all. Hold thy owne there wench, and I warrant thee. Sir, he that is accuſtom'd to deceiue. Gaines this reward by it when he ſpeakes truth, Not to be credited. No indeed ſir. Doe you thinke ſir, if I intended any ſuch thing, I would haue forewarned you? The old Gentleman did but dreame ſo. Alaſſe good Gentleman, I told him how other wo men vſed their husbands, but I would conforme my ſelfe to obedience. Pray let me ſpeake one word with him in private. Tis not a thing Sir, of that deare expenſe: Though you were pleaſd to tax me for that crime ▪ 'Tis onely this, time was, I could not loue you; Though reaſon ſince, has rectified my iudgement, And clear'd my eyes, that I can ſee my good. Then I confeſſe I made a ſolemne oath, None ſhould enioy my loue; but he that durſt Attempt to ſteale mee; this is not intended, For any perill to you, but for ſafeguard Of my firſt vow, which I muſt needs performe. Now if you pleaſe to come at a ſet houre, None but your ſelfe, and fetch mee, I will yeeld To goe with you, whither you ſhall command.
speeches.Aemi: O my diſtracted thoughts, and the raſh counſell Of lone and hatred, when they are oppos'd By avarice of parents, that confine Their childrens fancies to there ſordid mind. Were the bright ſunne their of spring, they would joyne him, Vnto the earth, if gold might be ingendred. Wee in our ſelues haue no part, if debard The election of our love, and our condition Is worſe then beaſts, whoſe will acknowledgeth No check in that; the Turtle takes her mate Without compulſion, and in Summers prime, Each bird will chuſe out her owne Valentine. A fire, 'tis a fooliſh one, that leades you without the precinct of your gravity, I ſtrange, a man of your judgement ſhould talke ſo prepoſterouſly. O Maſter Careleſſe here has beene your Vncle A woing to me.
No Miſtreſſe of yours Sir, yet if you aske nothing but what I pleaſe to anſwer, you may.
speeches.Dot: Let it not ſeeme ſtrange to you that I have felt this transformation, your forme has wrought a miracle vpon me, the pulchritude of your feature, that is able to extract youth out of age, and could make Aeſon young againe, without the helpe of Medea, it has put a fire into mee, and I muſt impute it neither to Herbes, nor Philtrums, but to the influence, and power of your beauty.
Bring me to that, and ile yield to any thing. You ſhall pardon me: he is my ſonne I hope, as well as yours, and he ſhall bee faſhion'd after my humour: why, ſhould you thinke to hinder my proſpect from looking to him? I ſay he ſhall ranke with the beſt, ſpend his money and learne breeding. No you ſhall keepe him ſtill at home with you; he ſhall not dare to enlarge his Charter, to haue any more wit then his father, let him ſit in the ſhop with nere a paire of cuffs on his hands, and play at Fox and Geeſe with the fore man, entertaine cuſtomers, with a diſcourſe as moatheaten as your cloath, and not be able to looke upon a Lady, but court ſome filly creature of his owne tribe, with ſpeeches out of bookes, ten times worſe then any remnant; and after ſupper ſteale abroad and be drunke in feare, this you can be content with. Well, when he was a child, it was the prettieſt talking thing, and the wittieſt withall, the neighbours tooke ſuch delight to heare it. There was a good Knight lay in my houſe then was ſo kind to him, but you nere knew the reaſon, ſince you haue cleane marr'd him that's apparant. Yes when tis too late; and the cuſtome of ruſticity is growne into an other nature with him, when his mind is ſetled upon the Lees of it, and the edge of his humour quite taken off, when learning has brought downe his ſpirit, then you'l repent his reſtraint; has he not a pretty ingenuity? So much the better, I would haue it ſo, giue him meanes to performe it, ſhew your ſelfe a loving father, and be true in your propheſie. Within there, call your young Maſter hither Crot chet, hee has beene all this day at his ſtudy, makes the boy mopiſh with his ſcholerſhip, for want of better exerciſe; as revelling, courting, feaſting, and the like, be ſtands plodding and muſing as if his eyes turn'd with a wire, it has poyſond his very complexion, he is growne fallow with it, I know not what would become of him, if I did not ſometimes put mo ney in his purſe, and ſend him abroad, to ſinne for his recrea tion. No, Ile teach you what tis to anger a woman that brought a Dowry with her. See what a Picture of formality you haue made of him, come hither ſonne Lackwit, what booke haue you there? What be the Armes ſonne? Well ſaid ſonne, ſtand for the credit of the houſe. I that he is ile be ſworne, the Fondlings are as good Gentlemen, as any be in the Citie, the boy has a Parlous head, how ſhould he find out this I marvaile? Yet husband, I never ſaw you weare one in my life. Loe you there, can you bee content thou man per verſe to all reaſon, having a ſonne of ſo large and proſperous hopes, that might ſtand up the glory of his kindred, of ſuch pregnancie of wit and underſtanding, ſo rich in the qualities that can beare up a Gentleman, to let him ſinke, and not che riſh him with thoſe helpes that might advance his gallantry. You haue had your floriſhing ſeaſon, and are now withered, your bloſſomes of beauty are blowne off & therefore muſt be content out of that dry ſtalke to afford ſome ſap to maintaine his ſucceſſion; pray how many young Gentlemen haue you in this Towne, that goe in pluſh, and their fathers to plow in the countrey? ſhall we haue worſe Preſidents in the Citie? impart I ſay, and giue him twenty peeces, and when they are gone giue him twenty more. Will you diſparadge him, as if he knew not what to doe with it? doe you thinke that Fencers, Dancers, Horſe matches (Ile haue him verſt in all theſe, and omit nothing that may demonſtrate his breeding;) beſides Miſtreſſes, and implements that belong to them require, nothing? What iſt? A medicine. Then you are right. Doe any thing, for the improuement of your diſcipline. Come Crotchet. How now what's the matter? How comes this about? How was it ſonne? Doe, tell the ſtory, Crochet. Nay but ſhew vs the manner of it. And will you be angry with him for this? 'twas well done, take no wrong of them, better looſe all the cloathes off from his backe, then to keepe a cloake for his cowar diſe. What is it ſonne? Well husband, giue it this once, and Ile vrge you no more, lets ſee how the Boy will imploy it. Nay, but giue it him for my ſake, I am confident he has a good project; you have example for it in your trade. How many haue you, that breake dayly, and yet their freinds ſet them vp two or three times one after an other? Muſt Crochet goe with you? How ſhould one ſpeake with him? As how, good Maſter Doctour? Pray relate ſome of them. Yes good Sir, let us heare them. How did you heale him ſir? That was excellent. You tooke a hard taske in hand, M r Doctour. O monſtrous! How did you heale him ſir? How did you with him ſir? Ile remember this ifaith. How did you reclaime him? Husband that was exellent, was it not? Good ſweet Fido conduct him in, and goe along with him, that if any heereafter ſhall be ſo averſe, in his ignorance, to all goodneſſe, as to queſtion this miracle, you may be pro duc'd as a witneſſe. Why Ile ſtay heere, and expect my ſonne Lackwit, with his project. He ſent mee word he would come preſent ly, and ſee where he enters. How now ſonne Lackwit; whither away ſo furious? Why were you at cardes ſonne? Tell vs how was it ſonne? You put vs too much into a longing, ſonne. How ſo ſonne? That he ſhall, Ile ſee that done upon my word.
This is a booke of Heraldry forſooth, and I doe find by this booke that the Lackwits are a very ancient name, and of large extent, and come of as good a Pedegree, as any is in the Citie; beſides they haue often matcht themſelues into very great families, and can quarter their Armes, I will not ſay with Lords, but with Squiers, Knights, Aldermen, and the like, and can boaſt their deſcent to be as generous, as any of the Lafooles, or the Iohn Dawes whatſoever. The Lackwits Armes, why they are three Aſſes ram pant, with their eares prickant, in a field Or, and a Rams head for their creſt, that's the Armes. Nay, I will uphold it beſides, though my father be a Citizen, yet I am a Gentlemans ſonne by the mothers ſide. Find it out, as if I were ſuch a foole, I did not know my owne Coat. Ile tell you father if I lift now; I can goe twenty degrees backe like a crab, to find out the tracke of our genti lity. To no purpoſe at all, but I know, what I purpoſe to doe with it. I purpoſe to make a medicine of it. I deſire ſir to incorporate my ſelfe into your ac quaintance. And they would but learne me to ſweare and take Tobacco, tis all I deſire. That mother wit that put them in my head, has put money in my purſe, and as farre as that money will leade me, I will be bold and wiſe: I have my humours, and I ſcorne the pollution of the Mechannicks. What, I will beare my ſelfe like a Gentleman. Now doe I want ſome two or three good oaths, to expreſſe my meaning withall. Any thing I, you ſhall make a blowing horne, or what you liſt of me. I muſt pay all, muſt I? And all at my charges? Yes, I have a Taylor that will truſt mee for any thing that Ile have him. Pray explain that rule to me, I do not underſtand you. Tis very well, is this all? O I ſhall doe this to a haire, and by the ſame con ſequence I ſhall be a Captaine ſomtimes: ſhall I not? Then good Captaine let's have a Dance, for theſe Gentlewomens ſakes; beſides there be many that come to ſee nothing elſe. What a queſtion is there to a man of quality? Yes I can dance, and that ſome that are here ſhall ſee and feele before we part; for I meane to ſhake my heeles with that fervour, that it ſhall ſtrike them into a fit of my love, ſhall be worſe then any ague to them. What tune Captaine? I am afraid this dancing will breed ſpavins in my legs, this caper has put me in remembrance of a clicke in my back, I got at my laſt vaulting. O Lord Captain, nine ſuch hornets are able to ſting a man to death. Who I? O Lord brother Captaine, I have not the third part of it. What to doe Captaine? Why Gentlemen, I hope you will not uſe me ſo, 〈◊〉 your brother, why Gentlemen. Good Crochet helpe me downe, I ſhall breake my necke elſe. I know not, an ill houre of the brotherhood, Ile after them with a vengeance. Who I pay the recknoning? 'Slight I came but now in. S'death the Captaine is gone away with my Hat, and my cloake too, I tell thee Ile pay no reckoning. What ſhall I doe Crochet? I ſo I will, come ſir, Ile goe in and talke with your Maſter. What is't Crochet? So I will Crotchet. Maſſe thou wert not with us at the firſt neither. Thou mightſt haue carried Away two or three of the Captaines oaths with thee. Oh Crotchet, I am thinking now, how brauely ile liue, when my father is dead. Let Crochet relate. I ſcorne to be the trumpet of mine owne valour, I. Well mother, if you will giue mee twenty pound more, Ile doe you ſuch a peece of ſervice, that you ſhall thanke mee for it as long as you live. Nay you ſhall not know, before it be done: the concluſion ſhall crowne it. I warrant you, come Crochet. Yes, tis a buſineſſe that can not be done by one alone ▪ HOw doe I looke now Crochet? Well, and thou art ſure there is but one of them, and he comes diſguis'd like Dotario, to ſteale away my ſiſter? That man that has done ſo ſhall thinke of me and this place as long as he lives for it: Goe and give warning Crochet, that no man withſtand me, unleſſe he be weary of his life. I long to exerciſe my puiſſance: thou art ſure there is but one of them? ſtand by a little, and let me flouriſh with my ſword, to animate my ſpirits; now whatſoever hee is, that comes in my way, I pronounce him to be a miſerable mortall. What haſt thou there Crochet. Give by Crochet, till I queſtion them: it behooves a wiſe man to deal with words, before he deſcend to blowes: what arrant knight are you ſir? and whither doe you travell with that Damoſell? No ſir, I doe not guard, nor regard any man, and yet Ile ſtand upon my guard, and this is the poynt Ile main taine. How, I your brother? No, I ſcorne to have af fiance with ſuch a conny-catcher: you ſir Neſſus, deliver up your theft, or I will play the Hereules with you. I, ſhe is my ſiſter, but you are a counterfeit, and have ſtolne her away. Thou villaine, doſt thou not know, if I were dead, and her other ſiſter, ſhe would be next heire, and then thou mightſt be hangd for her? I, this Gentleman has, but you have abus'd him, and tooke his wrong name upon you. I am conſidering with my eye, which part of him I ſhall firſt cut off. A match. Let's lay hold on him; what is he gone? how finely might my father have been cheated, and all wee now, if I had not beene: that's ſome roguing Servingman diſguis'd Ile lay my life on't; if I be not fit to be chronicled for this act of diſcretion, let the world judge of it. Well Crochet, when I have marryed her to the right party, if my father does not give me forty pounds more, he ſhall marry the next daughter himſelfe. So I will Crochet, come let us to the Church. Crochet, bid them ſtay without, till I call for them. Make roome there, and let ſuch produce there Game, that haue good cardes to ſhew. I am ſure all the wit and valour I had, was at ſtake for it. There was old ſhuffling and cuting amongſt them, and I had not ſpied their knavery they might haue put a tricke vpon vs, faith. No, I was at dice. I came the Caſter with ſome of them I thinke, and I had like to haue made their bones rattle for it. There was a Rooke would haue gone at In and In with my ſiſter, if I had not made a third man, he would haue ſwept all away, and wiped our noſes when he had done. No matter how; but if I haue not playd the wiſe man now, and done an act worthy of applauſe, let mee bee hiſt off for my labour. If it be no more thankes worthy, Ile tell you at my leaſure, when you haue prepar'd your vnderſtanding. Peace ſirrah, Ile haue no man tell it but my ſelfe, becauſe the prayſe of it belongs wholy to mee; and I could but effect halfe a dozen more ſuch exployts, Ide write my owne Commentaries. Well I am content to open the ſluſes of your hap pineſſ • ; let them in Crochet, but take heed you be not too gree dy of it, leſt the ſodaine joy overwhelme you. O muſt you ſo ſir? Well, there they are Barke and Tree, but as I am a hairy beaſt, if I had not been, they had been as farre a ſunder, as Temple barre and Algate. Why Ile ſhew you. there was an other Changling as like to him in ſhape, as Iupiter to Amphitrue, nay if I ſhould ſay, as I am to, let mee ſee what? That would haue married her in his ſtead, and car ried her away, if I had not prevented them. Crotchet I would thou wert a poſt, that I might beat out my braines againſt thee. Well I would know, how all theſe things had come to ſo good perfection but for me now.
Nay ſir they are condemn'd, that's certaine, you haue paſt your iudgement upon them, and my young Maſter muſt execute it. Then farewell ſir. Come, be not diſmaid, what ere you ſay, Ile ſweare it: you muſt affirme you loſt your hat And cloake in a skirmiſh. Why what if I had ſir? I can coyne them my ſelfe without any treaſon I warrant you. Yes, pray let me heare you. Nothing but the fortune of the warres forſooth: my young maſter has beene in as ſtout a fray as ever the Geni us of Fleetſtreet trembled at. Come ſir uncaſe, your ſelfe; tis no glory for you to lurke any longer under the perſon of ſuch a wretch. Pray ſir will you get him his cloake and hat againe that he loſt in the skirmiſh. Nay, if fortune ſhould not favour ſuch as you and I are, ſhee would leaue her old wont.
Stay husband, Ile go with you: but harke you ſon Lack wit, doe you know to what purpoſe this gold was given you? And why would you ſir, knowing this before, Suffer your daughter to be abus'd by him? Now by my life, I thinke, and 'twere not for me, You'd wind your ſelfe into ſuch Labyrinths, You'd not know how to extricate your ſelfe.
Yes I will diſſolue it into Aurum potabile, and drinke nothing but healths with it. Nay I will domineer, and haue my humors about me too. Stay Crotchet, doe you perceiue nothing? you dull animall looke here. No, I will not giue, nor lend a friend a penny, there's no ſuch confutation of a mans being a Gentleman; but when I am drunke, and haue my wine and my whores about me, Ile ſpend twenty or thirty ſhillings upon you, but I will not giue you a penny Crotchet. You know where to come to me, you ſhall find me in my pentificalibus. I haue drawne the map of it already: Ile goe every day in my cloake lind with pluſh, and my bever hat, Ile keepe my whores, and my running horſes, and ile maintaine thee in as good a pyed livery, as the beſt footman of them all goes in. Adviſe me good Crochet.
How, make her mad, what doe you expect from that: what can you gaine by the loſſe of her wits? And doe you prize The ſatisfying of a lewd deſire So much, to rob your Miſtris of her ſenſes? Can you accuſe her of inconſtancy? Or taxe her of diſhoneſty? Or will you Prove falſe to her? what miſcief do you intend? What hopes can you conceive, that may ſecure So great a ſinne from Heavens juſt puniſhment? Have you a drug or incantation, And thinke to make her ſenſeleſſe of her griefe, With the privation of her underſtanding? If you doe, you muſt imploy Some other meſſenger. Let me adviſe you Keep her in her right mind while you have her: Love of it ſelfe is an illuſive ſpirit, And will enough diſtract her without helpe. Then men begin to underſtand their good, When they have loſt it, and an envious eye Seekes after vertue when it is extinct, That hated it alive. Sir you ſpeake truth, upon my knowledge that, He is as ſlippery, as an Eele, in love, And wriggles in and out, ſir, at his pleaſure; He can as eaſily diſpenſe with vowes, As ſweare them; and can at a minutes warning, If an occaſion ſerve, ſupply himſelfe With a continuall, and freſh entertainment Of a new Miſtris. Nay he is a rare man, And has done many and ſtrange Cures ſir.
Sir he ſhall command my heart and hand on his occaſions, Ile as ſoone draw in his quarrell, as to piſſe againſt a wall.
He ſhall be able to paſſe through the needles of all occurrences. I ſay by Hermes, he that has a fortune, And power to acquaint the world with his perfections, And ſeekes to ſmother them, let him dye wretched. Captaine, what thinke you, ſhall he be a brother? By Saint George he that dyes ſo, dyes valiantly.
speeches.Cap,: Prithee let it alone, by that element it charmes me into melancholly.
Sir you have built a ſconce ſince you came in of thirty pounds, and before you have any more, my Maſter in tends to be ſatisfyed. You muſt ſtay and pay the reckoning firſt, beſides the Muſicians expect ſomthing. That's all one, you were all of a neſt, they are flowne away, and there's none left but your ſelfe. Tis all one to me, if you can ſatisfy my Maſter ſo.
What Gentlemen be theſe Captaine? Where's the money? I haue not ſix-pence in the world, the Cobler had all I had, for mending of your boots. Why if theſe Gentlemen come to beſtow a Supper on you, let them giue me money aforehand. I tell you I haue not a penny in the houſe. Yes and turne mee behind the dore for my reckoning; You haue ſerv'd me ſo I know not how often, no I haue truſt ed you too much already: you haue not payd me a penny for your lodging, ſince you came to my houſe, beſides what I haue lent you out of my purſe. Yes, you care not what becomes of any thing. Why can you not aske them for money? You haue more ſignes in your head, then hang at all the Alehouſes in towne againe. I tell you I can not doe it, nor I will not.
speeches.Lack ▪: Let him expect my fury Crochet. I will batter any man that ſhall come neere me, my fiſt is like a Sling, my head like a Ram, and my whole body an Engine, and I will make any man toothleſſe that ſhall offend me.
An ordinary diſeaſe, and cure, in ſome things I am of an opinion that Stertinius The Stoick was, who held all the world mad.
